payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are both giraffes and the substantial surrounding scene represented through drawn contours, interior marks and shading rather than retained photographic rendering?
node.criteria: Pass if drawn contours, interior marks and constructed shading represent both giraffes and substantial surrounding regions. Evaluate the giraffes' bodies, spots and legs separately from the vegetation, hills, sky and ground; neither region alone establishes satisfaction. Broad directional strokes and blended drawn shading may represent simplified environmental forms without preserving fine detail. Fail if substantial areas in either region still depend on retained photographic surface detail or photographic modeling, with only added outlines, grain or blur. Distinguish photographic modeling through retained source-specific detail and tonal structure not re-expressed by drawn marks; accurate anatomy, detailed spots, smooth gradients, dark shading and source resemblance are not by themselves proof of photographic rendering. Texture and smudging alone establish neither drawing nor photography. Return unknown only when evidence is unavailable or genuinely insufficient to distinguish the rendering, not simply because different regions provide different evidence.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images for the requested chalk-drawing transformation. Examine whether the giraffes' contours, body shading and markings are re-expressed as drawn forms, and whether vegetation, hills, sky and ground are independently represented by drawn marks and shading rather than merely softened source detail.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s binding already captures the key regions, but its broad “represented by drawn marks” test appears to over-credit a stylized finish. The traces repeatedly cite outlines, spots, broad strokes, and chalk-like grain, then infer that the whole scene is drawn; they do not separately test whether substantial regions still retain photographic structure. In the edited image, the giraffes and nearby vegetation show clear drawn treatment, while the hills, sky, and ground are largely smeared into broad tonal fields, with source composition and some photographic modeling still apparent. Refine the decision criterion to assess each region independently and distinguish constructed marks/forms from blur, smudging, or texture alone; require evidence that substantial environmental areas have actually been re-expressed, not merely softened. Keep the whole-image completion judgment separate from evidence of partial progress, so strong animal treatment cannot automatically make the entire transformation a pass. The repeated high-confidence “yes” traces despite the partial reference suggest a systematic criterion/binding gap, not a transport or dependency failure; do not treat repetition or confidence as proof of completion."}
